To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
social network sites are networked publics where youth engage in public performance, identity work, and socializing.

youth are using social network sites as "networkedpublics" to gather and socialize with their friends and peers, and that the unique properties of these sites (persistence, searchability, replication, and invisibility) affect the way youth interact and build their social lives.

youth use social network sites for friendship-making and socialization; that they are aware of and use properties of networked publics for their purposes; and that they are active participants in creating and sustaining the culture of networked public life.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how youth make meaning and build culture through their engagement with networked publics.
how networked publics are being used by youth to create and maintain peer culture, and the ways in which the properties of these networked publics affect the ways in they are used.
how youth use networked technologies to negotiate the social and cultural spaces in which they are embedded.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
social network sites like My Space and Face Book have been created to allow people to interact and share ideas with one another.
social network sites are not merely the new "hottest" thing to do, but rather they are a reflection of the social and cultural climate in which they are being used.
social network sites are a new type of networked public, one that is mediated by computer networks and software.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the social network site is the new mall, and that teens are using it to build their social world in the same way that they used malls in the past.
the networked public is a new social form that has emerged in the digital age.
youth use networked social spaces to create a public presence for themselves and to connect with other youth.
The main takeaway from our work is that

networked publics are not just sites for socializing with peers, but also serve as sites where teens learn about the culture of the Internet and develop a sense of their own identities as Internet users.
social network sites are not merely a technological innovation, they are a social form, and they must be understood through the lens of social practice.

youth are using these networked publics for a variety of purposes that go well beyond the "self expression" and "self presentation" that have been the focus of much of the popular and academic discourse on these sites.
